source_text:
Ἐπίστασθε γὰρ καὶ καλῶς ἐπίστασθε τὰς ἱερὰς γραφάς, ἀγαπητοί, καὶ ἐγκεκύφατε εἰς τὰ λόγια τοῦ θεοῦ. πρὸς ἀνάμνησιν οὖν ταῦτα γράφομεν.
Μωῦσέως γὰρ ἀναβάντος εἰς τὸ ὄρος καὶ ποιήσαντος τεσσαράκοντα ἡμέρας καὶ τεσσαράκοντα νύκτας ἐν νηστείᾳ καὶ ταπεινώσει, εἶπεν πρὸς αὐτὸν ὁ θεός: Κατάβηθι τὸ τάχος ἐντεῦθεν, ὅτι ἠνόμησεν ὁ λαός σου, οὓς ἐξήγαγες ἐκ γῆς Αἰγύπτου: παρέβησαν ταχὺ ἐκ τῆς ὁδοῦ ἧς ἐνετείλω αὐτοῖς, ἐποίησαν ἑαυτοῖς χωνεύματα.
καὶ εἶπεν κύριος πρὸς αὐτόν: Λελάληκα πρός σε ἅπαξ καὶ δὶς λέγων: Ἑώρακα τὸν λαὸν τοῦτον, καὶ ἰδού ἐστιν σκληροτράχηλος: ἔασόν με ἐξολεθρεῦσαι αὐτούς, καὶ ἐξαλείψω τὸ ὄνομα αὐτῶν ὑποκάτωθεν τοῦ οὐρανοῦ, καὶ ποιήσω σε εἰς ἔθνος μέγα καὶ θαυμαστὸν καὶ πολὺ μᾶλλον ἢ τοῦτο.
καὶ εἶπεν Μωϋσῆς: Μηδαμῶς, κύριε: ἄφες τὴν ἁμαρτίαν τῷ λαῷ τούτῳ, ἢ κἀμὲ ἐξάλειψον ἐκ βίβλου ζώντων.
ὢ μεγάλης ἀγάπης, ὢ τελειότητος ἀνυπερβλήτου. παρρησιάζεται θεράπων πρὸς κύριον, αἰτεῖται ἄφεσιν τῷ πλήθει, ἢ καὶ ἑαυτὸν ἐξαλειφθῆναι μετ’ αὐτῶν ἀξιοῖ.
thought_title: Moses intercedes for Israel after the golden calf
orientation: The Roman church is writing to the Corinthians, reminding them of Scripture examples of intercession and self-sacrifice, and now turns to Moses pleading for Israel after the golden calf.
pass_a_gloss: For you know and know well the sacred writings, beloved, and you have bent over into the oracles of God. For remembrance therefore these things we write. For Moses having gone up into the mountain and having done forty days and forty nights in fasting and humility, God said to him: Come down quickly from here, because the people of you has broken the law, whom you led out from the land of Egypt: they turned aside quickly from the way which you commanded to them, they made for themselves molten images. And the Lord said to him: I have spoken to you once and twice saying: I have seen this people, and behold it is stiff-necked: allow me to destroy them, and I will wipe out the name of them from under the heaven, and I will make you into a nation great and wonderful and much more than this. And Moses said: By no means, Lord: forgive the sin to this people, or also me wipe out from the book of the living. O of great love, O of perfection unsurpassable. A servant speaks boldly to the Lord, he asks forgiveness for the multitude, or also himself to be wiped out with them he deems worthy.

choices.why: Literal rendering of the Greek; 'scriptures' would be anachronistic here since the author uses a descriptive phrase rather than a technical term
The verb means to stoop or bend down toward something, suggesting close, attentive study; 'bent over' preserves the physical image
The noun denotes a state of being brought low, not the virtue of humility; 'humiliation' captures the self-afflicting condition of Moses' fast
The noun refers to cast-metal objects, specifically the golden calf; 'molten images' is the standard literal rendering
Strong negative interjection expressing refusal; 'by no means' preserves the force of Moses' protest
The verb means to speak with frankness and boldness; 'speaks boldly' captures the servant's daring before the Lord

bible_refs.note: Κατάβηθι τὸ τάχος ἐντεῦθεν, ὅτι ἠνόμησεν ὁ λαός σου... ἐποίησαν ἑαυτοῖς χωνεύματα

pass_b_english: You know the sacred writings well, dear friends, and you have bent over the oracles of God. So I am writing these things to remind you.

When Moses went up the mountain and spent forty days and forty nights in fasting and humility, God said to him: “Go down from here quickly, because your people, whom you led out of the land of Egypt, have broken the law. They have quickly turned aside from the way you commanded them, and they have made molten images for themselves.”

And the Lord said to him: “I have spoken to you once and twice, saying: I have seen this people, and look, they are stiff-necked. Let me destroy them, and I will wipe out their name from under heaven, and I will make you into a great and wonderful nation, far more numerous than this one.”
But Moses said: “By no means, Lord. Forgive the sin of this people, or else wipe me out of the book of the living.”
What great love! What unsurpassable perfection! A servant speaks boldly to the Lord, asks forgiveness for the multitude, or even asks to be wiped out along with them.

problems.quote: considers it right to be wiped out
problems.source_quote: ἢ καὶ ἑαυτὸν ἐξαλειφθῆναι μετ’ αὐτῶν ἀξιοῖ
problems.why: 'ἀξιοῖ' means 'asks/requests/demands', not 'considers it right'; Moses requests his own destruction, not judges it proper.
problems.fix: or even asks to be wiped out along with them
problems.ruling: ἀξιοῖ means 'requests/demands'; 'considers it right' misrepresents Moses asking/deeming himself worthy to be wiped out.

edits.old: or even considers it right to be wiped out along with them
edits.new: or even asks to be wiped out along with them

problems.why: Glossary requires 'humility' for ταπεινοφροσύνη; here ταπεινώσει is cognate but contextually 'humility' or 'lowliness' expected.

fixed: The English already says exactly what the source says for the final sentence; no change needed.

problems.why: Frequent switching between 'Master' and 'Lord' for God may seem intentional but lacks consistency.
problems.fix: Standardize divine titles or explain the variation.

edits.old: What great love! What unsurpassable perfection! A servant speaks boldly to his Lord, asks forgiveness for the multitude, or even asks to be wiped out along with them.
edits.new: What great love! What unsurpassable perfection! A servant speaks boldly to the Lord, asks forgiveness for the multitude, or even asks to be wiped out along with them.

fixed: The problem about 'Master' vs 'Lord' is not present in the English: the English consistently uses 'Lord' for God in this passage. No change needed.

last_rejected.why: The English attributes the first speech to 'God' and second to 'the Lord'. Source has ὁ θεός then κύριος. This is accurate. No error.
last_rejected.ruling: Reporter confirms English 'God'/'Lord' matches source ὁ θεός/κύριος. No error.

last_rejected.quote: far more numerous than this one
last_rejected.why: πολὺ μᾶλλον ἢ τοῦτο means 'much more/greater than this one', referring to the nation. 'Numerous' is added — the Greek says 'great and wonderful' already, and 'much more than this' refers to greatness, not specifically number. The LXX has 'πολὺ καὶ θαυμαστὸν' — wait, let me re-read: ποιήσω σε εἰς ἔθνος μέγα καὶ θαυμαστὸν καὶ πολὺ μᾶλλον ἢ τοῦτο. 'πολὺ' here is 'much/great', not 'numerous'. 'Far more numerous' adds 'numerous' which is interpretive. But 'much more than this' could mean greater in every sense. The English 'far more numerous' is too specific. However, 'numerous' is a possible sense of πολύς. Actually πολὺ μᾶλλον ἢ τοῦτο = 'much more than this [one]'. The 'numerous' is not in the Greek. But 'much more' could refer to greatness. This is a slight over-interpretation but within range. No major error.
last_rejected.ruling: πολὺ μᾶλλον ἢ τοῦτο: 'numerous' is within range of πολύς applied to ἔθνος. Not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: So I am writing these things to remind you.
last_rejected.why: The plural γράφομεν is the church speaking; English makes a single writer the author.
last_rejected.fix: So we are writing these things to remind you.
last_rejected.ruling: γράφομεν is first-person plural, but the epistolary plural commonly refers to a single author (1 Clement 53); "I am writing" is within normal range, meaning unchanged.
